# GOALS — the standing goal, the subgoal tree, and the rule that keeps the loop running
Status: **DESIGN.** This page defines the goal artefact and its rules; it ships no code. The first seeded `goals.jsonl` and any writer tooling are separate board work. Until that row lands, the factory's standing goal exists nowhere — which is the defect this page closes.

## 1. The problem
The word "goal" appears in the doc set exactly twice, and both times it is not a definition: inside the owner quotation at `specs/FLEET-MEMORY.md:24` ("…the goal is that the main hermes can search for things that have hapend across the fleet"), and as the section heading "Scope and non-goals" at `specs/TRACE.md:103`. No page says what the factory's top-level goal IS, what subgoals hang beneath it, how a subgoal is closed, or why the loop keeps running.
The owner asked for the artefact, verbatim (board row CF-345, 2026-11-22):
> *"i want the top level goal and the subgoasl that would need to be"*
and for its ending:
> *"the last subgoal is a loop so it keeps you going for ever"*
The typos are the owner's; both quotes are cited verbatim and are the requirements. Everything below follows from those two sentences: one standing goal, a tree of subgoals beneath it, every subgoal closing on evidence — except the last one, which by design never closes.

## 2. The artefact — `goals.jsonl`
The goal artefact is one file: `.coding-hermes/goals/goals.jsonl`. It lives beside the board (`.coding-hermes/board/tasks.jsonl`, `AGENTS.md` §"The board"), is git-tracked, and is **append-only**: one JSON object per line, UTF-8, LF-terminated. The board is the work; this file is the direction the work serves. A board row that cannot name the goal record it advances is a row without a rudder — allowed, but suspect.
Three record types, all carrying `type`, `seq`, `at` (ISO-8601 UTC) and `by`:
| type | fields | written when | |---|---|---| | `goal` | `id` (`GOAL-<n>`), `title`, `statement`, `non_negotiables` (array), `status` (`active` or `closed`) | the goal is opened; a later line with the same `id` and `status:"closed"` is the only close | | `subgoal` | `id` (`G<n>`), `goal` (parent goal id), `parent` (subgoal id or `null`), `title`, `kind` (`terminal` or `loop`), `status` (`open`, `closed` or `superseded`); a close adds `closed_at`, `evidence`, `run_id`; a supersession adds `superseded_by` | the tree grows; a later line with the same `id` updates the mutable fields | | `decision` | `id` (`D<n>`), `goal`, `text`, `chosen`, `alternative` | a direction is settled (the goal-and-subgoal-tracking rule: every decision carries what it beat) |
`seq` is a file-unique, monotonically increasing append ordinal — it, not file order alone, is what the queries in §6 sort by. A minimal file:
```json {"type":"goal","seq":1,"at":"2026-11-22T17:00:00Z","by":"owner","id":"GOAL-1","title":"ship the factory","statement":"turn the template into a self-running fleet","non_negotiables":["no root","every check names the measured value"],"status":"active"} {"type":"subgoal","seq":2,"at":"2026-11-22T17:00:00Z","by":"owner","id":"G1","goal":"GOAL-1","parent":null,"title":"provision a node","kind":"terminal","status":"open"} {"type":"subgoal","seq":3,"at":"2026-11-22T17:00:00Z","by":"owner","id":"G2","goal":"GOAL-1","parent":"G1","title":"keep producing work for ever","kind":"loop","status":"open"} {"type":"decision","seq":4,"at":"2026-11-22T17:00:00Z","by":"owner","id":"D1","goal":"GOAL-1","text":"loop cadence","chosen":"scheduled tick","alternative":"session-only autopilot"} ```

## 3. The subgoal tree
A goal's subgoals form a tree: `parent: null` roots it, any `subgoal` id parents the lines that name it, and sibling order is `seq` order — the tree reads top to bottom in append order. The subgoal ids are file-unique across all goals (`G1..` is not reused for a second goal).
**Laws (normative):**
- **GL-1 Append only.** A correction is a new line with a higher `seq`; no line is rewritten, reordered or deleted. This is the board's own rule (`AGENTS.md`: "Append only") applied to direction instead of work. - **GL-2 Ids are file-unique.** A re-stated id may change only the mutable fields (`status`, `waits_on`, `closed_at`, `evidence`, `run_id`, `superseded_by`); a different `goal` or `parent` under the same id is a defect — supersede it with a new id instead. - **GL-3 Every goal ends in the loop.** A goal's tree carries at least one `terminal` subgoal, and its LAST subgoal (highest `seq`) is exactly one `kind:"loop"` subgoal, which has no children. This is the owner's sentence made structural: the loop is what comes after all the finite work. - **GL-4 Evidence is a locator.** A `closed` subgoal line names a commit sha, a board row id (`CF-nnn`), an audit or report path, or a `run_id`. Prose is not evidence (the traceability rule, `specs/TRACE.md` §2 rule 4, applied to goals). - **GL-5 A goal cannot close under an open subgoal.** A `goal` line with `status:"closed"` MUST NOT be appended while the closure gate (§5) exits non-zero. This is the artefact's one hard invariant. - **GL-6 The loop has no closure condition.** No tool, lane, cron or judge may close or auto-close the loop subgoal, and it carries no deadline or iteration cap. Only an owner decision (`decision` record) supersedes it.

## 4. Closing a subgoal
A `terminal` subgoal closes by appending its own id again with `status:"closed"`, `closed_at`, and the evidence locator of GL-4 — normally the board row that shipped it (a subgoal becomes rows; that is how goal-and-subgoal-tracking phrases it), or the commit digest of a spec landing. A subgoal that is abandoned rather than done is `status:"superseded"` with `superseded_by` naming the decision id (or the replacing subgoal id) — a supersession is recorded history, not an erasure.

## 5. The closure invariant — the gate
The current state of a subgoal is the line with its id and the highest `seq`. The gate below is what GL-5 means operationally; run it before flipping a goal to `closed`, for that goal's id (GOAL-1 from the §2 example):
```bash jq -se 'map(select(.type=="subgoal" and .goal=="GOAL-1")) | group_by(.id) | map(max_by(.seq)) | all(.status != "open")' .coding-hermes/goals/goals.jsonl ```
Exit `0` — every subgoal of the goal is `closed` or `superseded`; the goal line may flip to `status:"closed"`. Exit `1` — at least one subgoal is `open`; the flip is refused. These are the measured behaviours of this exact program (2026-11-22, against the §2 shape with one subgoal closed and the loop open: `false`, exit 1; after the loop's supersession line: `true`, exit 0). `jq -e` derives the exit code from the truthiness of the last output, so an empty tree (a goal with no subgoals at all) vacuously passes the gate and is caught by GL-3 instead — the shape check in §6 must also pass.

## 6. The termination rule
**Terminal subgoals terminate; the loop does not.** A terminal subgoal's only exit is its closure record (§4). The loop subgoal implements the owner's second sentence: on its cadence it produces the next unit of work regardless of board state, has no success condition, no timeout and no iteration cap. Its non-termination is **by design, not a defect** — quoting the owner again: *"the last subgoal is a loop so it keeps you going for ever"*. It MUST NOT be "fixed" by adding an auto-close, a deadline or a max-iterations clause; a change that makes the loop terminate is a change to the owner's requirement and needs an owner decision first.
Stated plainly, the consequence of GL-5 plus GL-6: a goal whose tree ends in a loop subgoal NEVER reaches `status:"closed"`. The factory keeps going for ever. That is the intended behaviour, not a bug to chase. Stopping the system is an owner act: a `decision` record, then a supersession line for the loop subgoal (`status:"superseded"`, `superseded_by` the decision id), after which the §5 gate can pass and the goal may close. A loop that is not firing is a stall, not a termination — repair it (§7), never redefine it.
The shape checks, for the same example file:
```bash # the last subgoal of the tree is the loop (GL-3) — must print "loop" jq -sc 'map(select(.type=="subgoal")) | sort_by(.seq) | last | .kind' .coding-hermes/goals/goals.jsonl ```

## 7. The skills that implement the loop
The goal loop is not hypothetical machinery; five skills on this host implement it, and they are the named implementors of this artefact:
| skill | path | role in the loop | |---|---|---| | `autopilot-goal-execution` | `$HOME/.hermes/skills/autonomous-ai-agents/autopilot-goal-execution` | drives one goal to done inside a session: every turn advances a subgoal or reports a verified stop condition | | `self-driving-work-loops` | `$HOME/.hermes/skills/autonomous-ai-agents/self-driving-work-loops` | the machinery that keeps producing work between sessions; it implements the loop subgoal's cadence, and its own trigger text quotes the owner's "keeps going forever" sentence | | `hermes-persistent-goals` | `$HOME/.hermes/skills/devops/hermes-persistent-goals` | arms and diagnoses `/goal` and `/subgoal`; reads the session GoalState out of `state.db` | | `hermes-goal-loop-ops` | `$HOME/.hermes/skills/devops/hermes-goal-loop-ops` | repairs a stalled or wrongly armed session goal loop — the stall path of §6 | | `goal-and-subgoal-tracking` | `$HOME/.hermes/skills/devops/goal-and-subgoal-tracking` | turns an owner direction into the artefact's content: one living goal with `G1..Gn` subgoals and `D1..Dn` decisions |

## 8. Querying
The artefact is queryable with plain `jq` — no tooling ships with this page. From the repo root, against `.coding-hermes/goals/goals.jsonl`:
```bash # the goals, in their current state jq -sc 'map(select(.type=="goal")) | group_by(.id) | map(max_by(.seq))' .coding-hermes/goals/goals.jsonl
# every subgoal's current state, tree order jq -sc 'map(select(.type=="subgoal")) | group_by(.id) | map(max_by(.seq)) | sort_by(.seq)' .coding-hermes/goals/goals.jsonl
# the open subgoals jq -sc 'map(select(.type=="subgoal")) | group_by(.id) | map(max_by(.seq)) | map(select(.status=="open"))' .coding-hermes/goals/goals.jsonl
# the §5 closure gate for GOAL-1 jq -se 'map(select(.type=="subgoal" and .goal=="GOAL-1")) | group_by(.id) | map(max_by(.seq)) | all(.status != "open")' .coding-hermes/goals/goals.jsonl ```
`group_by(.id)` collapses each id's history lines; `max_by(.seq)` picks the current one; the close and supersede fields sit on that line. Any lane or the control host can enumerate the goal and its subgoal states with these four programs, and GL-5 is checkable by anyone.

## 9. Scope and non-goals
The **session-level** goal loop has its own runtime state: `state.db`, table `state_meta`, key `goal:<session_id>`, a JSON GoalState (`goal`, `status`, `turns_used`/`max_turns`, `subgoals`, `contract`, `gates`, `last_verdict`, …) — the shape documented by hermes-persistent-goals and hermes-goal-loop-ops, which correctly state that this state is "NOT a config file and NOT a goals table". That is true of the session loop's runtime and does not compete with this page: the session GoalState is **derived** from `goals.jsonl` when a session is armed with `/goal`, and this file is the authority the derived state serves. A session GoalState that contradicts `goals.jsonl` is a bug in the arming step, not a second definition of the goal.
goal-and-subgoal-tracking keeps its living goal document out of the product repo "until the owner decides where the work ships". For the factory the ship target is decided — it is `specs/GOALS.md` for the rules and `.coding-hermes/goals/goals.jsonl` for the records; that skill's document sections (status line, NON-NEGOTIABLES, `G1..Gn`, `D1..Dn`) map onto the record fields of §2.
Out of scope: the first seeded tree and any writer helper (board work); arming crons and cadences (self-driving-work-loops' own territory); the scheduler's admission model (`docs/SCHEDULER-ADMISSION.md`); and the board itself — goals are direction, rows are work, and `goals.jsonl` never becomes a second work queue.
